questions.stem: Which function of the respiratory system directly contributes to blood pH control?

choices.text: Changing the amount of CO₂ exhaled
Increasing the O₂ concentration in inspired air without changing ventilation
Increasing hemoglobin saturation independent of CO₂ transport
Altering respiratory rate without changing arterial CO₂ levels

questions.explanation: Ventilation controls CO₂, which is linked by equilibrium to H⁺ and bicarbonate.

questions.stem: Which structure belongs to the upper respiratory system as defined in these lectures?

choices.text: Nasopharynx
Larynx
Trachea
Primary bronchus

questions.explanation: The course groups the nose, sinuses, nasal cavity, and pharynx as upper respiratory structures; larynx and lower airways are lower.

questions.stem: Which part of the respiratory tract is normally devoted to conduction rather than direct gas exchange?

choices.text: Terminal bronchioles
Respiratory bronchioles
Alveolar ducts
Alveoli

questions.explanation: Terminal bronchioles end the conducting portion; the first alveoli appear at respiratory bronchioles.

questions.stem: How does pulmonary ventilation differ from gas diffusion?

choices.text: Ventilation moves air in bulk; diffusion moves individual gas molecules down partial-pressure gradients
Ventilation is diffusion in alveoli; gas diffusion is movement of the diaphragm
Ventilation is movement of blood through lung capillaries; diffusion is movement of air in the trachea
Ventilation and diffusion both require ATP-driven pumps through the respiratory membrane

questions.explanation: Pressure-driven bulk flow moves air, while microscopic gradients drive alveolar and tissue exchange.

questions.stem: Which activity is an additional respiratory function rather than a step of oxygen delivery?

choices.text: Sound production using vocal folds
Diffusion of oxygen across the alveolar wall
Ventilation that delivers air to alveoli
Oxygen loading onto hemoglobin in pulmonary capillaries

questions.explanation: The larynx generates voiced sound using exhaled air.

questions.stem: Which sequence correctly describes the basic route of inspired air?

choices.text: Nose or mouth → pharynx → larynx → trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli
Nose → pharynx → trachea → larynx → bronchi → alveoli
Nose → larynx → pharynx → bronchioles → bronchi → alveoli
Nose → pharynx → larynx → bronchioles → trachea → alveoli

questions.explanation: Air passes from the pharynx through the larynx and trachea before branching through the bronchial tree.

questions.stem: Which statement distinguishes internal respiration from cellular respiration most accurately?

choices.text: Internal respiration concerns gas exchange with tissues; cellular respiration concerns metabolism that uses O₂ to produce ATP
Internal respiration is the exchange between alveoli and blood; cellular respiration is gas exchange between blood and tissue
Internal respiration means moving air through the trachea; cellular respiration means binding O₂ to hemoglobin
Internal respiration is mitochondrial ATP generation; cellular respiration is diffusion at systemic capillaries

questions.explanation: The terms name different processes; the lecture sometimes presents both together for teaching.

questions.stem: Why do nasal conchae help condition inspired air?

choices.text: They increase mucosal contact and airflow mixing
They make the alveolar diffusion membrane much thinner
They change the diameter of the glottis during inspiration
They provide skeletal muscle contraction to drive the incoming airflow

questions.explanation: Conchae create convoluted pathways, improving contact with warm, moist mucosa.

questions.stem: What are the choanae?

choices.text: Posterior openings from the nasal cavity into the nasopharynx
Paired openings from the larynx into the trachea
Air pores between alveoli
The openings between true vocal folds

questions.explanation: The internal nares/choanae connect the nasal cavity with the nasopharynx.

questions.stem: Which structure is made chiefly of bone and separates the front of the mouth from the nasal cavity?

choices.text: Hard palate
Soft palate
Uvula
Epiglottis

questions.explanation: The hard palate forms the bony anterior partition; the soft palate is muscular posteriorly.

questions.stem: What distinguishes the nasopharynx from the lower two pharyngeal subdivisions?

choices.text: It primarily conveys air and is behind the nasal cavity
It opens directly into the esophagus rather than the nasal cavity
It contains the primary bronchi and carina
It is the region between the tongue base and epiglottis

questions.explanation: The nasopharynx is superior, above the soft palate and behind the nasal passages.

questions.stem: What is the main role of vibrissae?

choices.text: Trap relatively large particles near the nostrils
Move mucus up the trachea by beating rhythmically
Produce the humidifying fluid on the alveolar surface
Detect airborne odor molecules with olfactory neurons

questions.explanation: Nasal hairs filter larger material at the nasal vestibule.

questions.stem: What connects the nasopharynx to the middle ear for pressure equalization?

choices.text: Pharyngotympanic tube
Alveolar duct
Thoracic duct
Nasolacrimal duct

questions.explanation: The auditory/Eustachian tube runs between middle ear and nasopharynx.

questions.stem: Which observation is a defensible benefit of nasal compared with mouth breathing?

choices.text: Incoming air is warmed, humidified, and filtered by the nasal passages
It bypasses the conducting airways so air reaches alveoli faster
It produces surfactant before air reaches the larynx
It removes all inhaled particles, unlike mouth breathing

questions.explanation: Nasal airway conditioning prepares the air for delicate lower airway surfaces.

questions.stem: Which pairing best describes respiratory mucosa?

choices.text: Epithelium above an underlying lamina propria
Respiratory epithelium above alveolar capillary endothelium
Visceral pleura above lung parenchyma
Goblet cells above a continuous layer of tracheal cartilage

questions.explanation: The conducting airway mucosa consists of a lining epithelium and supporting loose connective tissue.

questions.stem: What is the primary direction of mucus movement in the mucociliary escalator?

choices.text: Toward the pharynx
Down toward the respiratory bronchioles
Outward through the alveolar-capillary membrane
From the pharynx into the esophagus during every inspiration

questions.explanation: Coordinated ciliary beating transports trapped debris upward for swallowing or expulsion.

questions.stem: Why does the epithelial lining become very thin at the alveoli?

choices.text: Minimize the diffusion distance for gas exchange
Withstand the mechanical abrasion of swallowed food
Provide more sites for cartilage attachment
Increase airway mucus storage capacity

questions.explanation: Simple squamous type I cells create a thin gas-exchange barrier.

questions.stem: Which epithelial type is characteristic of much of the nasal cavity and larger conducting airways?

choices.text: Pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium
Keratinized stratified squamous epithelium everywhere
Transitional epithelium
Simple squamous epithelium with no mucus cells

questions.explanation: Conducting airways often use ciliated, mucus-producing pseudostratified epithelium.

questions.stem: Which epithelial type is especially suited to abrasion in the oropharynx?

choices.text: Stratified squamous epithelium
Simple squamous epithelium
Simple cuboidal epithelium
Pseudostratified epithelium in every subregion

questions.explanation: Multiple layers offer protection at shared food/air passages.

questions.stem: A person whose airway cilia are severely impaired would most directly struggle with what?

choices.text: Removing mucus and trapped particles from conducting passages
Maintaining the affinity of hemoglobin for O₂
Keeping the alveolar basement membrane thin
Producing type II cell surfactant

questions.explanation: Ciliary transport is a key airway clearance mechanism.

questions.stem: Which airway is more commonly lined by simple cuboidal epithelium rather than cartilage-supported pseudostratified epithelium?

choices.text: Bronchiole
Main bronchus
Proximal trachea
Nasal cavity

questions.explanation: The epithelial pattern typically shifts toward simple cuboidal epithelium in small bronchioles.

questions.stem: Which group lists only the lecture's unpaired laryngeal cartilages?

choices.text: Epiglottis, thyroid, cricoid
Arytenoid, corniculate, cuneiform
Arytenoid, thyroid, corniculate
Cuneiform, cricoid, arytenoid

questions.explanation: Epiglottis, thyroid, and cricoid are unpaired; arytenoid, corniculate, and cuneiform occur in pairs.

questions.stem: What most directly produces voiced sound?

choices.text: Vibrations of the true vocal folds as air passes through the glottis
Vibration of the vestibular (false vocal) folds
Rotation of the thyroid cartilage without any fold vibration
Turbulence across an open glottis without vibration of the true folds

questions.explanation: Phonation requires vocal-fold vibration controlled by laryngeal muscles.

questions.stem: What is the principal task of the intrinsic laryngeal muscles?

choices.text: Adjust vocal-fold position and tension
Elevate and stabilize the entire larynx during swallowing
Raise air pressure by contracting the diaphragm
Protect the laryngeal inlet by secreting mucus

questions.explanation: Intrinsic muscles move the vocal apparatus; extrinsic muscles mainly position the larynx.

questions.stem: How does increasing vocal-fold tension generally affect fundamental pitch, with other factors held constant?

choices.text: It raises pitch
It lowers pitch in every circumstance
It eliminates the glottis
It changes only the loudness, never frequency

questions.explanation: Tighter folds usually vibrate at higher frequency; mass and length also influence pitch.

questions.stem: What is the epiglottis's defensive role?

choices.text: Help divert swallowed material away from the laryngeal inlet
Elevate the soft palate to block the nasopharynx
Actively vibrate to produce the speaking voice
Tighten the true vocal folds to increase pitch

questions.explanation: It participates with laryngeal elevation and fold closure in protecting the airway.

questions.stem: Which sequence captures the forceful cough mechanism?

choices.text: Close glottis, build intrathoracic pressure, suddenly open it to expel air
Keep the glottis fully open throughout pressure buildup
Inhale while keeping the glottis closed throughout the entire reflex
Close the glottis only after forceful air has already been expelled

questions.explanation: Compression against a closed glottis followed by sudden opening yields rapid expiratory flow.

questions.stem: What are the vestibular folds?

choices.text: False vocal cords located superior to true vocal folds
The true vocal folds involved in routine phonation
The aryepiglottic folds forming the sides of the laryngeal inlet
The laryngeal ligaments attached below the cricoid cartilage

questions.explanation: Vestibular folds contribute to protection, not the main mechanism of voiced sound.

questions.stem: What is the specific contribution of the arytenoid cartilages?

choices.text: Move the vocal folds to adjust the glottic opening
Form the C-shaped framework supporting the trachea
Create the recess between the tongue and epiglottis
Generate most of the sound through direct cartilage vibration

questions.explanation: Paired arytenoids act as movable anchors for vocal-fold positioning.

questions.stem: Why are tracheal cartilage rings C-shaped rather than fully circular?

choices.text: They maintain patency while allowing the esophagus behind the trachea to expand
They allow the posterior tracheal wall to become a second gas-exchange membrane
They permit the trachea to fully collapse during every quiet expiration
They prevent the trachealis muscle from changing airway diameter

questions.explanation: A posterior gap allows flexibility and accommodation for swallowing.

questions.stem: Where is the trachealis muscle found?

choices.text: Across the posterior opening of the C-shaped tracheal cartilages
Within the wall of the smallest respiratory bronchioles
Between the true and false vocal folds
Inside the muscular dome of the diaphragm

questions.explanation: This smooth muscle spans the posterior tracheal wall and can alter its diameter.

questions.stem: Which landmark marks the division into the two primary bronchi?

choices.text: Carina
Epiglottis
Uvula
Cardiac notch

questions.explanation: The carina is the internal ridge at the tracheal bifurcation.

questions.stem: Why are aspirated solid objects more likely to enter the right main bronchus?

choices.text: It is generally wider, shorter, and more vertical
It branches into three lobar bronchi, whereas the left branches into only two
Its airflow is always at a higher pressure than the left during inspiration
Its wall contains more cartilage plates than the left main bronchus

questions.explanation: The right main bronchus is anatomically more aligned with the tracheal axis.

questions.stem: Which structures supply individual lobes of the lungs?

choices.text: Secondary bronchi
Tertiary bronchi exclusively
Respiratory bronchioles exclusively
Alveolar ducts

questions.explanation: Lobar/secondary bronchi branch into each lung lobe; tertiary bronchi serve segments.

questions.stem: How do bronchioles differ from bronchi?

choices.text: Bronchioles lack cartilage and have smooth muscle regulating their diameter
Bronchioles contain large cartilage rings, but bronchi contain only smooth muscle
Bronchioles are alveoli with no smooth muscle, while bronchi have no epithelium
Bronchioles contain complete bony rings, while bronchi have flexible hyaline cartilage

questions.explanation: Bronchioles rely heavily on smooth muscle rather than cartilaginous support.

questions.stem: Which autonomic signal is associated with bronchodilation in the lecture?

choices.text: Sympathetic activation, especially β₂ adrenergic signaling
Parasympathetic muscarinic stimulation of bronchiolar muscle
Increased acetylcholine release from airway vagal nerves
Constriction of the smooth muscle surrounding bronchioles

questions.explanation: Adrenergic relaxation tends to increase bronchiolar radius, lowering resistance.

questions.stem: Why do terminal bronchioles differ from respiratory bronchioles?

choices.text: Terminal bronchioles conduct air without alveoli; respiratory bronchioles start bearing alveoli
Terminal bronchioles contain scattered alveoli, but respiratory bronchioles have none
Terminal bronchioles are supported by cartilage, but respiratory bronchioles are supported by bone
Respiratory bronchioles precede terminal bronchioles along the airway tree

questions.explanation: The respiratory zone begins as alveoli appear along respiratory bronchioles.

questions.stem: What is the main difference between the right and left lung lobation?

choices.text: Right has three lobes and left has two
Right has two and left has three
Each lung always has four lobes
Both lungs have one lobe without fissures

questions.explanation: The right has superior, middle, inferior; the left has superior and inferior.

questions.stem: Which fissure is found only in the right lung in typical anatomy?

choices.text: Horizontal fissure
Oblique fissure
Cardiac notch
Interlobular septum

questions.explanation: The right lung has horizontal and oblique fissures, while the left normally has an oblique fissure.

questions.stem: The cardiac notch is associated with which lung?

choices.text: Left lung
Right lung
Both lungs equally
Neither lung—it is a tracheal structure

questions.explanation: The heart indents the anterior left lung.

questions.stem: Which pleural layer directly adheres to the lung surface?

choices.text: Visceral pleura
Parietal pleura
Pericardial serosa
Nasal mucosa

questions.explanation: Visceral pleura covers lung; parietal pleura lines chest wall and diaphragm.

questions.stem: What is normally inside the pleural cavity?

choices.text: A very thin film of lubricating serous fluid
A thick air pocket separating pleural layers under normal conditions
A layer of mucus produced by goblet cells
An alveolar surfactant reservoir around each lobe

questions.explanation: The pleural cavity is a potential space containing a thin film of fluid.

questions.stem: What crosses the lung hilum?

choices.text: Bronchi, blood vessels, lymphatics, and nerves
Only pulmonary arteries but not veins or airways
Only the main bronchus, with no vessels or nerves
Alveolar ducts and individual alveoli from every lobule

questions.explanation: The hilum forms the portal for the root structures of each lung.

questions.stem: Which airway supplies a bronchopulmonary segment?

choices.text: Tertiary (segmental) bronchus
Main (primary) bronchus alone
Alveolar sac
Nasopharynx

questions.explanation: Segmental bronchi define bronchopulmonary segments.

questions.stem: Which alveolar cells form most of the thin gas-exchange surface?

choices.text: Type I pneumocytes
Type II pneumocytes
Alveolar macrophages
Goblet cells

questions.explanation: Type I pneumocytes spread thinly across most alveolar surface area.

questions.stem: What is the main function of type II pneumocytes?

choices.text: Produce surfactant and help replace alveolar epithelial cells
Form the majority of the thin air–blood diffusion surface
Phagocytose debris as the principal dust-cell population
Move mucus toward the pharynx with motile cilia

questions.explanation: Type II cells produce the lipid-protein mixture that stabilizes alveoli.

questions.stem: Why is pulmonary surfactant essential?

choices.text: It reduces surface tension and limits alveolar collapse
It raises alveolar surface tension to generate expiration
It replaces hemoglobin as the primary O₂ carrier
It provides the ciliary drive for respiratory mucus clearance

questions.explanation: Lowering the tension of alveolar lining fluid keeps small air spaces more stable.

questions.stem: What do alveolar macrophages primarily do?

choices.text: Engulf inhaled debris and pathogens in air spaces
Secrete pulmonary surfactant into the alveolar lining
Form the extremely thin gas-exchange epithelium
Adjust the diameter of respiratory bronchioles by contraction

questions.explanation: Dust cells provide local phagocytic defense in alveoli.

questions.stem: Which layers represent the key respiratory membrane components in the lecture?

choices.text: Type I alveolar epithelium, fused basal laminae, and capillary endothelium
Type II pneumocytes, pleural mesothelium, and tracheal smooth muscle
Type I pneumocytes, surfactant only, and rib cartilage
Bronchiolar epithelium, airway mucus, and visceral pleura

questions.explanation: Diffusion crosses an unusually thin epithelial/basal-lamina/endothelial barrier.

questions.stem: Which property would most directly slow gas exchange across the respiratory membrane?

choices.text: Increased thickness of the exchange barrier
Reduced alveolar diffusion distance
Increased membrane surface area
A higher favorable partial-pressure gradient

questions.explanation: Greater distance obstructs diffusion; thinner and larger surfaces facilitate it.

questions.stem: Where are alveolar ducts situated?

choices.text: After respiratory bronchioles, leading toward clusters of alveoli
Between terminal and respiratory bronchioles, before alveoli appear
Between trachea and primary bronchi, near the carina
Within the pleural space as connective passages between lobes

questions.explanation: Alveolar ducts are distal air passages whose walls are largely alveolar openings.

questions.stem: According to Boyle's law, what happens to gas pressure if a fixed quantity of gas expands at constant temperature?

choices.text: Pressure decreases
Pressure increases
Pressure remains constant regardless of volume
Pressure becomes negative in absolute terms

questions.explanation: At constant T, P and V vary inversely (P₁V₁ = P₂V₂).

questions.stem: What initiates normal inhalation?

choices.text: Diaphragm and external intercostals contract, thoracic volume rises, alveolar pressure falls
Diaphragm relaxation raises thoracic volume and lowers lung pressure
Alveolar pressure rises above atmosphere before air is drawn inward
External intercostal contraction compresses the thorax to initiate inspiration

questions.explanation: Expanding the thoracic cavity lowers alveolar pressure relative to outside air.

questions.stem: Why is quiet expiration usually passive?

choices.text: Elastic recoil decreases lung volume when inspiratory muscles relax
It requires active abdominal muscle contraction on every resting breath
The diaphragm remains contracted throughout ordinary expiration
Inspiratory muscles actively squeeze the alveoli to expel air

questions.explanation: Recoil makes alveolar pressure transiently exceed atmosphere, causing outward flow.

questions.stem: When alveolar pressure is 759 mmHg and atmospheric pressure is 760 mmHg, what happens?

choices.text: Air moves into the lungs
Air moves out of the lungs
Air cannot move because pressures are similar
Blood moves into alveoli instead

questions.explanation: Air flows down the pressure gradient, from atmospheric to the slightly lower alveolar pressure.

questions.stem: Which muscles are the professor's two most important muscles of inspiration?

choices.text: Diaphragm and external intercostals
Diaphragm and internal intercostals only
External intercostals and sternocleidomastoid in every quiet breath
Abdominal muscles and internal intercostals

questions.explanation: These muscles expand the thoracic cavity during normal inspiration.

questions.stem: How does forced expiration differ from quiet expiration?

choices.text: It actively recruits expiratory muscles such as abdominal muscles and internal intercostals
It remains driven entirely by passive recoil, only faster
It recruits only the diaphragm, which contracts downward during exhalation
It is generated solely by opening the glottis without changes in thoracic pressure

questions.explanation: Forced expiration uses additional muscle work rather than simple recoil alone.

questions.stem: If bronchiolar radius decreases, what happens to airflow resistance, all else equal?

choices.text: Resistance increases markedly
Resistance decreases markedly
Resistance is unaffected by radius
Resistance only depends on blood pressure

questions.explanation: Small airways can strongly modulate resistance with smooth-muscle-induced diameter changes.

questions.stem: What is tidal volume?

choices.text: Air moved in or out during an ordinary resting breath
Air remaining after maximal expiration
Extra air inhaled after a maximal inspiration
Total air volume after maximal inspiration

questions.explanation: TV or VT describes the volume of an ordinary breath.

questions.stem: What is residual volume?

choices.text: Air remaining after maximal forced expiration
Air leaving with each normal breath
Extra inhaled air above a normal inspiration
The sum of inspiratory and expiratory reserve volumes

questions.explanation: RV remains even after a maximal breath out, preventing total lung emptying.

questions.stem: Which formula gives vital capacity?

choices.text: TV + IRV + ERV
TV + IRV + RV
RV + ERV
TLC + RV

questions.explanation: Vital capacity is maximum exhalable volume after full inhalation, excluding RV.

questions.stem: Which formula gives total lung capacity?

choices.text: VC + RV
VC − RV
TV + ERV only
IRV − TV

questions.explanation: TLC includes all air in the lungs at maximal inflation, including residual air.

questions.stem: What does the inspiratory reserve volume measure?

choices.text: Additional air inhalable above a normal tidal inspiration
Air remaining after maximal exhalation
The air exhaled in a resting breath
The air trapped in conducting bronchi alone

questions.explanation: IRV is the extra inhalation possible after an ordinary breath in.

questions.stem: Which quantity cannot be measured directly with ordinary spirometry alone?

choices.text: Residual volume
Tidal volume
Inspiratory reserve volume
Expiratory reserve volume

questions.explanation: Standard spirometry measures moved air and cannot directly capture air that stays after maximal expiration.

questions.stem: If ERV and RV are added together, what capacity results?

choices.text: Functional residual capacity
Vital capacity
Total lung capacity
Inspiratory capacity

questions.explanation: FRC is the lung volume remaining after a normal passive expiration.

questions.stem: What is a gas's partial pressure?

choices.text: Its individual contribution to the total pressure of a gas mixture
The fraction of gas stored permanently in tissue
The pressure exerted only by alveolar mucus
The same value as blood pH

questions.explanation: PO₂ and PCO₂ each reflect a component gas's pressure contribution.

questions.stem: What does Henry's law describe in respiratory physiology?

choices.text: The dissolved concentration of a gas is proportional to its partial pressure and solubility at constant temperature
That dissolved gas concentration is independent of its partial pressure
That equal gas partial pressures imply equal dissolved concentrations for all gases
That gases enter blood by active transport rather than dissolution

questions.explanation: Henry's law relates dissolved gas to pressure and its solubility properties.

questions.stem: Why does O₂ diffuse from alveoli into pulmonary blood?

choices.text: Alveolar PO₂ is typically higher than that of incoming deoxygenated pulmonary blood
Alveolar PO₂ is lower than incoming pulmonary venous PO₂
O₂ is transported by active pumps in alveolar macrophages
O₂ follows the CO₂ gradient rather than its own partial-pressure gradient

questions.explanation: Net diffusion follows the oxygen partial-pressure gradient across the exchange membrane.

questions.stem: Why does CO₂ diffuse from pulmonary capillaries toward alveolar air?

choices.text: Incoming blood PCO₂ exceeds alveolar PCO₂
Alveolar PCO₂ is greater than arriving pulmonary capillary PCO₂
CO₂ is actively pumped toward higher partial pressure in the alveolus
Hemoglobin carries CO₂ only as a dissolved gas and cannot release it in lungs

questions.explanation: CO₂ moves down a partial-pressure gradient from blood to alveoli.

questions.stem: Which pairing is correct for internal (systemic) gas exchange?

choices.text: O₂ from blood to tissues; CO₂ from tissues to blood
O₂ and CO₂ both from blood to tissues
CO₂ from blood to tissues; O₂ from tissues to blood
Neither gas crosses systemic capillaries

questions.explanation: Consuming tissues lower their PO₂ and generate CO₂, establishing complementary gradients.

questions.stem: If thick fluid or inflammation increases the alveolar diffusion distance, what is the expected effect?

choices.text: Gas exchange may become less efficient
Oxygen diffusion becomes faster because the surface is thicker
Gas exchange would continue at the same rate regardless of membrane thickness
Alveoli would no longer require a favorable partial-pressure gradient

questions.explanation: Exchange depends on the thickness, area, and gradients across the membrane.

questions.stem: What is oxyhemoglobin?

choices.text: Hemoglobin with oxygen bound to heme groups
Hemoglobin with O₂ removed from all binding sites
Hemoglobin carrying CO₂ attached to its globin chains
Hemoglobin bound to H⁺ without any O₂ molecules

questions.explanation: HbO₂ names oxygen-carrying hemoglobin.

questions.stem: Why does the oxygen–hemoglobin saturation curve have a sigmoidal shape?

choices.text: Cooperative binding changes hemoglobin's affinity as O₂ binds
O₂ binds to one heme site without affecting other sites
Each O₂ binding site becomes progressively less available regardless of occupancy
Blood PO₂ is constant across the alveolar and systemic circulation

questions.explanation: The hemoglobin tetramer's binding sites influence one another.

questions.stem: What favors O₂ unloading in active, CO₂-producing tissues?

choices.text: Increased CO₂ and H⁺ lower hemoglobin oxygen affinity
Increased pH and lower CO₂ always lower affinity
O₂ release stops whenever tissue temperature rises
Higher local PO₂ always pushes oxygen out of hemoglobin

questions.explanation: The Bohr effect helps supply active tissues under more acidic, CO₂-rich conditions.

questions.stem: At high alveolar PO₂, what is expected of normal hemoglobin?

choices.text: A high fraction of available O₂-binding sites becomes occupied
Hemoglobin tends to unload most O₂ despite high PO₂
Hemoglobin cannot bind O₂ unless blood becomes acidic
Hemoglobin remains approximately half saturated at all alveolar PO₂ values

questions.explanation: High PO₂ favors hemoglobin oxygen loading on the flat upper part of the saturation curve.

questions.stem: Which explanation best connects tissue metabolism and hemoglobin behavior?

choices.text: Working tissues consume O₂ and produce CO₂/H⁺, favoring diffusion and hemoglobin unloading
Working tissues raise PO₂ and eliminate every H⁺ ion, causing O₂ release
Hemoglobin can transport oxygen only if tissues stop making CO₂
Tissue PO₂ is unaffected by cellular oxygen use

questions.explanation: Lower tissue PO₂ plus changes in pH and CO₂ help direct oxygen where needed.

questions.stem: How does oxygen dissolved in plasma differ from hemoglobin-bound oxygen?

choices.text: Dissolved O₂ directly determines PO₂ but is a small share of total O₂ content
Dissolved O₂ provides nearly all total blood O₂ content
Dissolved O₂ determines hemoglobin production rather than blood partial pressure
Hemoglobin-bound O₂ directly contributes to PO₂ in the same way as free dissolved O₂

questions.explanation: Dissolved gas contributes to partial pressure; most oxygen content travels bound to Hb.

questions.stem: In what form is most CO₂-derived carbon carried in blood?

choices.text: Bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻)
Free carbonic acid molecules only
Carbaminohemoglobin only
Oxygen bound to heme iron

questions.explanation: The lecture's ~70% pathway predominantly yields bicarbonate, after transient carbonic acid formation.

questions.stem: What enzyme accelerates the reversible hydration of CO₂ in red blood cells?

choices.text: Carbonic anhydrase
Carbonic acid dehydrogenase
Carbon monoxide dehydrogenase
Bicarbonate reductase

questions.explanation: Carbonic anhydrase rapidly links dissolved CO₂ with the H₂CO₃/HCO₃⁻ equilibrium.

questions.stem: What is the chloride shift?

choices.text: HCO₃⁻ exchanges with Cl⁻ across the red-cell membrane during CO₂ transport
Movement of oxygen into RBCs in exchange for chloride
Transfer of H⁺ out of plasma into the alveolar air
Exchange of chloride for PO₂ across the lung's pleura

questions.explanation: Bicarbonate exits RBCs in systemic tissues as chloride enters, with a reverse exchange at the lungs.

questions.stem: What happens to blood pH if CO₂ accumulates because ventilation is inadequate?

choices.text: It tends to fall as CO₂ drives H⁺ generation
Blood pH rises as more CO₂ produces less hydrogen ion
The bicarbonate buffer equilibrium does not respond to changes in CO₂
Retained CO₂ immediately neutralizes all existing H⁺

questions.explanation: The CO₂/bicarbonate reaction can increase H⁺ and lead to respiratory acidosis.

questions.stem: Why can hyperventilation increase blood pH?

choices.text: Excess CO₂ removal shifts the buffer equilibrium toward lower H⁺
Rapid breathing increases the arterial PCO₂ while decreasing pH
It removes bicarbonate directly through the alveolar membrane
It raises H⁺ concentration while lowering blood PCO₂

questions.explanation: Reducing arterial PCO₂ decreases carbonic acid-related acidity, potentially causing respiratory alkalosis.

questions.stem: How does CO₂ bind in carbaminohemoglobin?

choices.text: To amino groups on globin protein chains
To the iron atom of the heme oxygen-binding site
To plasma bicarbonate ions that then bind hemoglobin
To the alveolar epithelial membrane rather than the globin molecule

questions.explanation: Carbaminohemoglobin contains CO₂ chemically attached to globin, not to the heme oxygen site.

questions.stem: Which approximate division matches the lecture's CO₂ transport percentages?

choices.text: 70% bicarbonate pathway, 23% carbamino compounds, 7% dissolved
70% carbamino compounds, 23% bicarbonate, 7% dissolved
70% dissolved, 23% carbamino compounds, 7% bicarbonate
70% bicarbonate, 23% dissolved, 7% carbamino compounds

questions.explanation: These values are teaching approximations: predominantly bicarbonate, then protein-bound, then dissolved gas.

questions.stem: What brainstem region contains networks essential for breathing rhythm?

choices.text: Medulla oblongata
Cerebellar cortex only
Occipital visual cortex
Spinal dorsal horn alone

questions.explanation: The medulla houses interacting neuronal groups needed for automatic respiration.

questions.stem: Which choice best reflects the lecture's DRG versus VRG distinction?

choices.text: DRG emphasizes inspiratory control, while VRG is more engaged when respiratory demand increases
DRG is principally expiratory during quiet breathing, while VRG controls smell
DRG is a pontine center, and VRG is exclusively in the cerebellum
DRG and VRG are purely sensory receptors located in the carotid bodies

questions.explanation: This is the instructor's functional shorthand; modern medullary networks are more interconnected.

questions.stem: What is the main role of the pons in breathing?

choices.text: Modulate the timing and pattern of medullary respiratory activity
Drive contraction of the diaphragm directly without medullary or spinal pathways
Perform gas exchange by regulating the respiratory membrane
Measure dissolved blood oxygen within the pleural cavity

questions.explanation: Pontine centers shape transitions between inspiration and expiration.

questions.stem: In the older nomenclature used by the course, which center tends to facilitate sustained inspiration?

choices.text: Apneustic center
Pneumotaxic center
Cerebellar cortex
Carotid sinus baroreceptor

questions.explanation: Apneustic is a historical functional label for pontine inspiratory-facilitating mechanisms.

questions.stem: Which center in the older lecture naming helps limit or terminate inspiration?

choices.text: Pneumotaxic center
Apneustic center
Thyroid follicle
Alveolar duct

questions.explanation: The pneumotaxic label denotes inspiratory-limiting pontine influence.

questions.stem: Why do central chemoreceptors respond strongly to a rise in arterial CO₂?

choices.text: CO₂ alters brain extracellular/CSF pH, affecting chemosensitive neurons
They sense arterial O₂ mainly through alveolar air entering the medulla
CO₂ cannot cross the blood-brain barrier so pH is unaffected
The signal is generated by CO₂ binding directly to vocal-fold muscle

questions.explanation: CO₂ can influence CSF acidity, which central respiratory networks detect.

questions.stem: Which receptors are particularly important when arterial PO₂ falls markedly?

choices.text: Peripheral carotid-body chemoreceptors
Central chemoreceptors responding only to blood glucose
Airway stretch receptors responding to tidal volume only
Baroreceptors that primarily monitor arterial blood pressure

questions.explanation: Peripheral chemoreceptors contribute significantly to the response to reduced arterial O₂.

questions.stem: What nerve directly carries the primary motor drive to the diaphragm?

choices.text: Phrenic nerve
Vagus nerve, which primarily moves the diaphragm
Intercostal nerves supplying the diaphragm from thoracic segments
Recurrent laryngeal nerve supplying the diaphragm

questions.explanation: Motor neurons from C3–C5 form the phrenic nerve innervating the diaphragm.

questions.stem: Which term describes inadequate oxygen availability in tissues?

choices.text: Hypoxia
Hypercapnia
Phonation
Hyperpnea

questions.explanation: Hypoxia refers to tissue oxygen deficiency; arterial and tissue oxygenation are related but not identical.

questions.stem: Why is acute epiglottitis potentially life-threatening?

choices.text: Swelling can obstruct the laryngeal inlet and airway
It typically increases vital capacity without affecting airflow
It inflames the vocal folds but cannot narrow the airway
The obstruction occurs only in pulmonary alveoli

questions.explanation: Inflammation in this small upper-airway region can reduce airflow sharply.

questions.stem: Why does pneumonia frequently impair gas exchange?

choices.text: Inflammation and fluid in alveolar regions increase diffusion distance and impair ventilation
Alveolar fluid reduces resistance so diffusion becomes faster
It causes oxygen to be transported only in dissolved form
Pneumonia affects only cartilage and never the exchange surface

questions.explanation: Alveolar exudate, collapse, and impaired ventilation/perfusion interfere with exchange.

questions.stem: What is a central airway problem in cystic fibrosis?

choices.text: Thick, poorly cleared mucus promotes blockage and infection
Excessively dilute airway mucus moves too quickly toward the alveoli
Loss of all type I alveolar cells is the primary inherited defect
CFTR dysfunction increases mucociliary clearance beyond normal

questions.explanation: CFTR dysfunction disrupts airway surface hydration and mucociliary clearance.

questions.stem: What directly increases airflow resistance during many asthma episodes?

choices.text: Bronchial smooth-muscle constriction plus airway inflammation
Smooth-muscle relaxation that widens all bronchioles
A fall in airway mucus and inflammatory swelling
Reduced vagal tone causing sustained dilation rather than constriction

questions.explanation: Narrowed, inflamed airways resist airflow and cause variable obstruction.

questions.stem: Why can laryngitis make the voice hoarse?

choices.text: Inflamed vocal folds vibrate abnormally
Inflammation changes only the lung's alveolar gas pressure
Hoarseness results only from changes in nasal hair movement
The voice is formed entirely in the pharynx independently of vocal-fold vibration

questions.explanation: Swelling affects normal vocal-fold vibration and sound generation.

questions.stem: A gas moving across the alveolar wall toward blood is an example of what process?

choices.text: Diffusion rather than bulk ventilation
Ciliary transport
Vocal articulation
Active filtration through a lymph node

questions.explanation: Molecules cross the respiratory membrane down partial-pressure gradients; air movement in tubes is ventilation.

questions.stem: During swallowing, which structure helps close access to the nasopharynx?

choices.text: Soft palate
Cricoid cartilage
Lung hilum
Pulmonary surfactant

questions.explanation: The soft palate elevates, helping keep swallowed material out of the nasal passage.

questions.stem: Which paired cartilages sit atop the arytenoid cartilages?

choices.text: Corniculate
Cricoid
Thyroid
Epiglottic

questions.explanation: Corniculate cartilages are small horns attached to the arytenoids.

questions.stem: Why does intrapleural pressure matter for ventilation?

choices.text: It helps keep lung surfaces mechanically coupled to the chest wall through the pleura
It prevents pressure changes from being transmitted from the chest wall to the lungs
It is the pressure in alveoli rather than in the pleural space
It is always equal to atmospheric pressure during normal quiet breathing

questions.explanation: The pleural fluid interface and normally subatmospheric pressure allow chest expansion to expand lungs.

questions.stem: Which formula gives inspiratory capacity?

choices.text: TV + IRV
RV + ERV
VC + RV
TV + ERV + RV

questions.explanation: Inspiratory capacity combines a normal tidal inspiration and the extra inspiratory reserve after ordinary expiration.

questions.stem: At the same PO₂, which change would generally shift the Hb–O₂ dissociation curve to the right?

choices.text: Higher CO₂ and lower pH
Lower temperature and lower CO₂
Lower H⁺ and lower CO₂
Complete absence of hemoglobin in blood

questions.explanation: Increased CO₂/H⁺ decreases affinity, facilitating O₂ unloading; this is the Bohr effect.

questions.stem: Where does the bicarbonate-to-CO₂ reaction reverse to help eliminate CO₂?

choices.text: In pulmonary capillary blood as CO₂ diffuses into alveoli
Only in systemic tissue capillaries, where CO₂ is continuously taken up
In the airway lumen before it reaches alveolar blood
In pleural fluid where carbonic anhydrase replaces pulmonary circulation

questions.explanation: Reversible chemistry in blood regenerates diffusible CO₂ in the lungs.

questions.stem: Why can low arterial PO₂ stimulate breathing even though central receptors respond strongly to CO₂?

choices.text: Peripheral chemoreceptors sense the O₂ decrease and signal brainstem circuits
Central chemoreceptors directly detect O₂ declines more strongly than carotid bodies
Peripheral chemoreceptors monitor only airway stretch, not blood gases
Decreased arterial O₂ cannot alter brainstem respiratory drive

questions.explanation: Carotid and aortic bodies provide oxygen-sensitive input complementary to central CO₂/pH sensing.
